title: EMA Crossback
teaches: The EMA Crossback as we trade it: the first pullback into the rising short averages after a stock has turned up out of a decline (a Wedge Pop) or broken out, a hold day that reaches the zone and closes at or above the 20 EMA in the upper half of its range, the buy is the trade a few cents over the hold day's high within three sessions, the stop sits a few cents under the hold day's low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a loss at the stop is the system working.

walkthroughs.title: UAA, June 2015: the clean stair-step
steps: UAA, 2015. A leader pops on 1.5x volume on 06-05, then drifts back to its averages in just 2 quiet sessions.
The hold day reaches the zone and closes above the 20 EMA, 9 still above 20. Nothing is bought yet.
2015-06-16: it trades over the hold day's high. Buy at market, 40.82. Stop a few cents under the hold day's low, 40.17.
Failure mode: the hold day's low breaks. Instead 3R comes in 5 days. First sell: a judgment, into the push.

walkthroughs.title: MU, August 2025: the clean crossback that failed
steps: MU, 2025. A pop on 08-08 on 1.3x volume, a 3-day drift, a hold day on 08-18. It looks clean.
2025-08-19: buy 123.70, stop 120.63. The size came from that stop, so the loss is already planned.
On 08-20 it trades down to 113.46 and takes the stop. We take the loss.
It reached 3R and 5R weeks later without us. A new buy needs a new hold day and a new trigger.

questions.q: What is the EMA Crossback?
choices: Any pullback in a long uptrend
A cross of the 9 under the 20 EMA
The first retest after the pop
A close back over the 20 EMA
questions.answer: The first retest after the pop
questions.why: The first retest after the pop. A breakout can stand in for the pop. Kell defines it as the first time the stock retests its moving averages after a strong upward move. In our rules it holds the averages with the 9 still above the 20. One close back over the 20 EMA is only a pop setting up.
questions.lesson_line: The crossback is the first pullback to the averages after the pop.

wrong.A cross of the 9 under the 20 EMA: That is the opposite. If the 9 EMA crosses under the 20 EMA, there is no reason to be long.
wrong.Any pullback in a long uptrend: Only the first pullback after the pop is the crossback. A later rest is a different move.
wrong.A close back over the 20 EMA: One close back over the 20 EMA is a pop setting up, not a crossback. The crossback is the pullback after it.

questions.why: True. The crossback is the pullback after the pop that holds the averages with the 9 still above the 20.
questions.lesson_line: Hold the averages with the 9 still over the 20.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We buy once price trades a few cents above the hold day's ___.
questions.answer: high
questions.why: High. The buy is a market order once price trades a few cents above the hold day's high. Entries are market orders, and the trigger is the high, not the close, the low or the open. Touching the averages is not a trigger either.
questions.lesson_line: Buy a few cents over the hold day's high, not the touch.
questions.simple: We buy at market once price trades a few cents over the hold day's high.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, entries are market orders)

questions.q: We buy the moment price touches the averages, before buyers show up.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. We do not buy the touch. We wait for a hold day that closes strong, then buy the trade over its high. Buying the touch before buyers show is a named mistake, and Kell says always wait for confirmation that buyers are stepping in.
questions.lesson_line: No hold day, no trigger, no buy. Wait for buyers.
questions.simple: No. We wait for buyers to show up before we buy.

deeper.trap: The trap is the touch itself. Price reaching the averages looks like the setup, but nothing yet shows buyers. Wait for the hold day to close in the upper half, then buy over its high.

reasons: Kell is the only web source; the named mistake is on our card

questions.q: Where does the stop go on a crossback?
choices: A few cents under the 200-day average
A few cents under the hold day's low
A few cents under the 20 EMA line
At the hold day's low, to the penny
questions.answer: A few cents under the hold day's low
questions.why: A few cents under the hold day's low. The stop comes first, and the size comes from it. The rule is a few cents under the low, not exactly on it. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the hold day's low.

wrong.A few cents under the 200-day average: The stop goes under the hold day's low. The 200-day line decides which stocks we buy, not where the stop sits.
wrong.A few cents under the 20 EMA line: The stop goes under the hold day's low. That low can sit above or below the 20 EMA, so the line is not the stop.
wrong.At the hold day's low, to the penny: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.

questions.simple: The stop goes a few cents under the hold day's low, and the share size comes from that stop.

deeper.example: Example: UAA was bought at 40.82 with the stop set first at 40.17, which is 1.6% under the buy. The shares come from that stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3 and F62, stop first)

questions.story: A hold day just closed.

questions.q: With the 9 EMA under the 20 EMA, there is no reason to be long the stock.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. With the 9 EMA under the 20 EMA there is no reason to be long. Kell says the same of his 10-day and 20-day lines. A crossback holds the averages with the 9 still above the 20.
questions.lesson_line: Fast average under the slow one: no long.
questions.simple: Yes. When the fast average sits under the slow one, there is no reason to be long.

reasons: the 9 and 20 pair is our house text while Kell uses 10 and 20 (D-021)

questions.q: In Kell's cycle, which stage comes right before the EMA Crossback?
choices: The Base n' Break
The Wedge Pop
The Exhaustion Extension
questions.answer: The Wedge Pop
questions.why: The Wedge Pop. After the Wedge Pop, the stock often tests its moving averages again, known as the EMA Crossback.
questions.lesson_line: Pop first, crossback second.

wrong.The Exhaustion Extension: That comes late in the cycle, and a Wedge Drop follows it, not a crossback.
wrong.The Base n' Break: That is another pullback after the crossback, so it comes later.

questions.q: Kell says a Wedge Pop is not just a cross of the averages. What should you focus on?
choices: Its price bars and its volume
A close above the 50-day
A weekly close over the 10-week
A new 52-week high first
questions.answer: Its price bars and its volume
questions.why: Price bars and volume. Kell says many traders wrongly think a Wedge Pop is simply about crossing the moving averages. He says to focus on price bars and volume.
questions.lesson_line: A pop is price bars and volume, not just a cross.

wrong.A close above the 50-day: A close over one line is the same trap. Kell says to look at price bars and volume.
wrong.A weekly close over the 10-week: Kell names price bars and volume, not a weekly line.
wrong.A new 52-week high first: The pop is the first rally back through the averages after a Reversal Extension, not a new high.

questions.simple: Price bars and volume. A cross of the averages alone is not enough.

reasons: one Kell article carries the key
the pop window is still open (D-076)

questions.q: One close back over the 20 EMA is already a crossback.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. One close back over the 20 EMA is a pop setting up, not a crossback. The crossback is the pullback after the pop.
questions.lesson_line: A pop first. The crossback is the pullback that follows.

questions.q: What makes the last bar a hold day?
choices: Touches the averages and closes strong
The big up day of the pop itself
The day price first closes under the 20
Any day price touches the averages
questions.answer: Touches the averages and closes strong
questions.why: A hold day touches the averages and closes strong. It is the first session of the pullback. Its low reaches the zone, the area from the 9 EMA down to about 1% under the 20 EMA. It closes at or above the 20-day EMA, in the upper half of its range. A touch alone is not enough.
questions.lesson_line: A hold day touches the zone and closes strong.

wrong.The day price first closes under the 20: A hold day closes at or above the 20 EMA. A close under it is the opposite, and on above-average volume it ends the setup.
wrong.The big up day of the pop itself: The hold day is the first session of the pullback. The pop comes before it.
wrong.Any day price touches the averages: Touching is only half of it. The hold day must also close at or above the 20 EMA, in the upper half of its range.

questions.simple: The hold day dips into the area of the averages and still closes strong, at or above the 20 EMA.

deeper.trap: Touching the zone is only half of a hold day. One real example touched the zone with its low but closed in the lower 3% of its range. The close gave the day back, so it was not a hold day.

reasons: key rests on one proposed card line (x03), not an owner ruling
the hold day is a proposed criterion (xbk.hold_day)

questions.story: The day before a buy. Look at the last bar.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The hold day closes at or above the ___ EMA.
questions.why: 20. The hold day closes at or above the 20-day EMA, in the upper half of its range.
questions.lesson_line: The hold day closes at or above the 20 EMA.

questions.q: A crossback can also follow a breakout, not only a Wedge Pop.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. A breakout over a base's pivot or a key level may stand in for the pop. Kell wrote of pulling back to the crossback after a nice breakout.
questions.lesson_line: Pop or breakout, then the first pullback.
questions.simple: Yes. A breakout can stand in for the pop, and the first pullback after it can be a crossback.

reasons: one Kell line plus a proposed card line
the breakout stand-in is a proposed criterion

questions.q: A clean crossback under the 200-day average is fine for us.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Below the 200-day is a hard no for stocks. The one exception is indexes and ETFs built to magnify an index's moves, on a reversal extension or a parabolic long. A crossback is not a parabolic long, so the hold day must close above the 200-day. A clean shape does not lift the rule.
questions.lesson_line: No longs under the 200-day, crossback or not.
questions.simple: No, we do not buy a stock under its 200-day line, even when the crossback looks clean.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26, the 200-day line)

questions.q: What is the lowest RS rating we accept on a crossback leader?
choices: An RS rating of 50
An RS rating of 70
An RS rating of 80
An RS rating of 95
questions.answer: An RS rating of 80
questions.why: An RS rating of 80, in a strong group. We buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. A floor of 50 or 70 is not enough, and 95 asks for more than the rule needs. A high rating without a strong group is not enough either.
questions.lesson_line: Buy leaders: RS 80 or more in a strong group.

wrong.An RS rating of 50: Our rule asks for an RS rating of 80 or more, not 50.
wrong.An RS rating of 70: Our rule asks for an RS rating of 80 or more, not 70.
wrong.An RS rating of 95: The floor is 80, so 95 asks for more than the rule needs.

questions.simple: A crossback is for leaders, so we want an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C31, RS 80 or more)

questions.q: Bought at 96.51, stop at 94.17 (1R is the gap between them). Where is 3R?
questions.why: $103.53. One R is the fill minus the stop: 96.51 - 94.17. Add three of those to the fill: 96.51 + 3 x (96.51 - 94.17) = 103.53. 3R is a measuring stick, not an order to sell. The first sell is a judgment.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. It is a yardstick, not a sell order.
questions.simple: 3R is the fill plus three times the gap down to the stop, which is 103.53 here. It is a measuring stick.

reasons: computed key (3R price)
the first sell is the owner's D-013 judgment, not a fixed 3R sale

wrong.$101.19: Counted 3R up from the stop, which is only two R above the fill.
wrong.$99.51: Added three dollars to the fill. 3R is three times the risk, not three dollars.
wrong.$105.87: Added four R, counting the fill as the first one.

questions.story: Bought on the trigger day.

questions.q: Fill 116.55, stop 112.39. How far under the fill is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 3.6%. The stop's distance is the gap over the fill: (116.55 - 112.39) / 116.55 x 100 = 3.6%. We prefer stops of 1 to 3% and call 3.5% good. Up to 5% is acceptable, so this one is wider than we like but fine to take.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the stop in percent. We like 1 to 3%, and up to 5% is fine.
questions.simple: The stop is 3.6% under the fill, a little past the 3.5% we call good, but under 5%.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A13, about 3%) and is tied to the pending D-005
fixed before (the old why leaned on size down past 3%)

wrong.4.2%: Used the dollar gap as if it were the percent.
wrong.0.36%: A decimal slip, one place too far left.
wrong.96.4%: Gave the stop as a share of the fill, not the gap between them.

questions.story: Bought on the trigger day.

questions.q: Account 90,000, risk 0.6%, buy 116.55, stop 112.39. The position cap is not reached. How many shares?
questions.answer: 129 shares
questions.why: 129 shares. Dollars at risk are 90,000 x 0.6%. Risk per share is the buy minus the stop: 116.55 - 112.39. Divide the first by the second and round down to 129. The position cap can only make the size smaller.
questions.lesson_line: Shares come from the stop: dollars at risk divided by risk per share.
questions.simple: Shares equal the dollars at risk divided by the gap between the buy and the stop, rounded down.

reasons: computed key (shares from risk)
rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, size from the stop)

choices: 151 shares
1,298 shares
772 shares
129 shares

wrong.151 shares: Divided the risk dollars by the stop's percent, not by the dollars per share.
wrong.772 shares: Divided the account by the price and ignored the stop.
wrong.1,298 shares: Typed the risk as ten times too big, so the share count came out ten times too big.

questions.story: Bought on the trigger day.

questions.q: A hold day's high is 64.00, its low 61.00, its close 63.40. How far up its range did it close, in percent (0 is the low, 100 the high)?
questions.why: 80%. The close above the low is 63.4 - 61. The range is 64 - 61. So (63.4 - 61) / (64 - 61) x 100 = 80%. That is in the upper half, where a hold day must close.
questions.lesson_line: A strong hold day closes in the upper half of its range.
questions.simple: The close is 80% of the way up the day's range, so it sits in the upper half.

reasons: computed key
the hold day is a proposed criterion (xbk.hold_day)

wrong.99%: Divided the close by the high. That ignores the low.
wrong.20%: Measured down from the high instead of up from the low.
wrong.3.8%: Divided by the close, not by the day's range.

questions.q: The 20 EMA is 100.00 and the hold day's low is 99.20. How far under the 20 EMA is the low, in percent?
questions.why: 0.8%. The low is under the 20 EMA by (100.00 - 99.20) / 100.00 x 100 = 0.8%. That is inside the zone, which runs down to about 1% under the 20 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: The zone reaches about 1% under the 20 EMA. Measure it.
questions.simple: The low is 0.8% under the 20 EMA, which is inside the zone that ends about 1% under it.

deeper.counter: The zone is a range, not a single line. It runs from the 9 EMA down to about 1% under the 20 EMA. A deeper undercut falls outside it. Another hold day had its low 2.1% under the 20 EMA, so it was outside.

reasons: computed key
the zone depth is a proposed criterion (xbk.depth)

wrong.99.2%: Gave the low as a share of the 20 EMA, not how far under it sits.
wrong.8%: A decimal slip. The low is under one percent below the line.

questions.q: Keep the alert, or drop it?
choices: Keep it; the high may still break
Keep it, but only through Friday
Drop it; the setup has gone stale
Buy Friday's break at half size
questions.answer: Drop it; the setup has gone stale
questions.why: Drop it. With no trigger within 3 sessions of the hold day, the setup is stale. Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday passed without a break of Monday's high. A late break is not this setup, and a smaller size does not bring it back.
questions.lesson_line: Three sessions to trigger. After that, start over.

wrong.Keep it; the high may still break: With no trigger within 3 sessions of the hold day, the setup is stale. The window has closed.
wrong.Keep it, but only through Friday: Friday is past the 3 sessions, and the setup is already stale. A short extension does not bring it back.
wrong.Buy Friday's break at half size: Friday is past the 3 sessions, so the setup is stale. A smaller size does not reopen the window.

questions.story: The hold day printed on Monday. By Thursday's close the stock has not traded over Monday's high.
questions.simple: Drop the alert, because three sessions passed with no trigger and the setup is stale.

deeper.example: Count the sessions. Monday is the hold day. Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday are the three sessions to trigger, and none of them traded over Monday's high. After Thursday's close the setup is stale.

reasons: key rests on one proposed card line (x08)
the 3-session window is tied to the pending D-003 (trigger)

questions.q: Buy tomorrow's break of the high?
choices: Yes; the hold day is clean
Yes, but only at half size
No; a report is too close
No; the 3-session window is spent
questions.answer: No; a report is too close
questions.why: No. We make no new buy if a report is due within 3 sessions, and this one is due in 3. A clean hold day does not lift the rule, and a smaller size does not either. The 3-session window to trigger has only just started, so it is not the reason.
questions.lesson_line: Check the report date before every buy.

wrong.Yes; the hold day is clean: The rule is no new buy if a report is due within 3 sessions, whatever the hold day looks like.
wrong.Yes, but only at half size: The rule bars the new buy. It does not allow a smaller size.
wrong.No; the 3-session window is spent: The hold day closed today, so the 3 sessions to trigger have not run yet. The report is the reason.

questions.story: The hold day closed today. The company reports in 3 sessions.
questions.simple: No, because we make no new buy when a report is due within 3 sessions.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22, no new buy within 3 days of a report)

questions.q: Which name fits?
choices: EMA Crossback; the first retest
20 EMA Pullback; a tap of 20
Wedge Pop; first close over
Breakout; a push to new highs
questions.answer: EMA Crossback; the first retest
questions.why: EMA Crossback. It is the first test of the averages after the stock's strong move back over them, which Kell calls the crossback. A tap of a 20 EMA that has been rising for weeks is the 20 EMA Pullback. This stock came out of a three-month correction.
questions.lesson_line: First test after the pop is the crossback. A tap of a long-rising 20 EMA is a pullback.

wrong.20 EMA Pullback; a tap of 20: That is a tap of a 20 EMA that has been rising for weeks. This stock had just come out of a three-month correction.
wrong.Wedge Pop; first close over: The pop was nine sessions ago. This is the first pullback after it.
wrong.Breakout; a push to new highs: This stock is testing its averages after the pop, not pushing out to a new high.

questions.story: A hold day just closed. A three-month correction ended nine sessions ago, with a pop on 1.7x volume. The 9 is over the 20 again. Today it dips back to those averages. It has not been near them since the pop.
questions.simple: This is the first test of the averages since the stock closed back over them, so it is the crossback.

reasons: rests on the held decision D-002 (crossback against the 20 EMA Pullback)

questions.q: Which stage is this?
choices: An EMA Crossback, a retest
A Wedge Pop, a first reclaim
A Base n' Break, later rest
A Wedge Drop, a break lower
questions.answer: A Wedge Pop, a first reclaim
questions.why: A Wedge Pop. One close back over the averages is a pop setting up, not a crossback. The crossback is the pullback after the pop. Kell says to read price bars and volume, not just the cross.
questions.lesson_line: A first reclaim is the pop. The pullback after it is the crossback.

wrong.An EMA Crossback, a retest: There has been no pullback yet. This is the reclaim itself.
wrong.A Base n' Break, later rest: That is a later rest in the cycle, after the crossback.
wrong.A Wedge Drop, a break lower: A Wedge Drop follows an Exhaustion Extension at the top of a run. This stock is turning up from weeks under its averages.

questions.story: After a three-month correction, the stock closes back over its 9 and 20 EMA on 1.7x volume.
questions.simple: This is the pop itself, the first move back over the averages. The crossback is the pullback that comes after.

deeper.counter: Counter: say the same stock later pulls back and holds its averages. If the 9 is still over the 20, that pullback is the crossback. Same stock, different day. The close back over the averages is only the pop.

reasons: the whole unit rests on Kell's definition (D-002)
the pop window is open (D-076)

questions.q: Crossback or Base n' Break?
choices: EMA Crossback; the first rest
Base n' Break; a later rest
Wedge Pop; the move before
Exhaustion Extension; a climax
questions.answer: Base n' Break; a later rest
questions.why: Base n' Break. The stock already pulled into its averages once, so this is a later rest. The crossback is the first rest after the pop, and Kell's name for a later rest is the Base n' Break. An Exhaustion Extension is a different stage, a climax far above the 9 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: First rest is the crossback. Later rests are Base n' Breaks.

wrong.EMA Crossback; the first rest: The crossback is the first rest. This is the second.
wrong.Wedge Pop; the move before: The pop was the move before the first rest.
wrong.Exhaustion Extension; a climax: An Exhaustion Extension is a climax run far above the 9 EMA. This stock is resting at its averages.

questions.story: A hold day just closed. The stock popped sixteen sessions ago and has already pulled into its averages once. Today it pulls back into them again.
questions.simple: The stock already rested at its averages once, so this second rest is a Base n' Break, not a crossback.

reasons: tied to the pending D-026 (a second pullback: Base n' Break or a graded-lower crossback)
fixed before (the old why said graded lower)

questions.q: A close under the 20 EMA on above-average volume ends the setup before the trigger.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. A close under the 20 EMA on above-average volume ends the setup before the trigger. That is the opposite of a hold day, which must close at or above the 20 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: A heavy close under the 20 EMA ends the idea.
questions.simple: Yes. A close under the 20 EMA on above-average volume ends the idea before we buy.

reasons: a proposed card line with no web source

questions.q: Is this a crossback buy?
choices: No; the 9 is still under the 20
Yes, if the stop is tighter
Yes; it is over the 50-day
No; it needs a gap up first
questions.answer: No; the 9 is still under the 20
questions.why: No. With the 9 EMA under the 20, there is no reason to be long. A crossback holds the rising 9 and 20 EMA with no run of closes under them. Retaking the 50-day does not fix that, and a tighter stop does not either.
questions.lesson_line: A stock that lost its averages is not a crossback.

wrong.Yes, if the stop is tighter: A tighter stop does not change the 9 being under the 20. There is still no reason to be long.
wrong.Yes; it is over the 50-day: Retaking the 50-day does not fix the short averages. With the 9 under the 20 there is no reason to be long.
wrong.No; it needs a gap up first: The hold day needs a low in the zone and a strong close, with the 9 above the 20. No gap is named.

questions.story: A stock popped weeks ago, then closed under its 50-day for nine sessions. Today it closed back above it. The 9 EMA is at 52.10 and the 20 EMA at 52.80.
questions.simple: No. The 9 is still under the 20, so there is no reason to be long, whatever the 50-day does.

reasons: the 9 and 20 pair is our house text while Kell uses 10 and 20 (D-021)

questions.q: Is this a crossback?
choices: No; it never got to the zone
Yes; the run was the pop
Yes; a tight drift will do
No; crossbacks need a pole
questions.answer: No; it never got to the zone
questions.why: No. The crossback's drift must reach the 9/20 zone. This stock jumped 32% in 12 sessions. Then it drifted six sessions well above the 9 and 20 EMA, so it never reached the zone. A big run before the drift does not change that.
questions.lesson_line: A crossback drift reaches the averages. A drift that stays well above them is not one.

wrong.Yes; the run was the pop: The drift must reach the 9/20 zone to be a crossback. This one stayed well above the 9 and 20 EMA.
wrong.Yes; a tight drift will do: A tight drift counts only if it reaches the 9/20 zone. This one never did.
wrong.No; crossbacks need a pole: The crossback needs no pole. Its drift must reach the 9/20 zone, and this one did not.

questions.story: A stock jumps 32% in 12 sessions. Then it drifts tight for six sessions, well above the 9 and 20 EMA.
questions.simple: Not yet. A crossback drift has to reach the 9 and 20 EMA zone, and this one stayed well above it.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line (x27) and the pending bull-flag pole option
fixed before (the pole was raised to 32% to clear the 30% option)

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Buy anyway on the old trigger
Buy a bit lower, under the low
Stand down until a new hold day
Keep waiting inside the 3 sessions
questions.answer: Stand down until a new hold day
questions.why: Stand down. The hold day's low broke before any trigger, so the setup is off until a new hold day forms. Buying the old trigger, buying under the low or waiting out the 3 sessions does not bring it back.
questions.lesson_line: Hold day's low breaks, setup off. Wait for a new hold day.

wrong.Buy anyway on the old trigger: The hold day's low broke before the trigger, so the setup is off and the old trigger no longer counts.
wrong.Buy a bit lower, under the low: The low broke, so the setup is off. A buy under the low is not this setup until a new hold day forms.
wrong.Keep waiting inside the 3 sessions: Once the hold day's low breaks before the trigger, the setup is off until a new hold day forms. The 3 sessions do not bring it back.

questions.story: Yesterday was the hold day. This morning, before any trigger, the stock trades under the hold day's low.
questions.simple: The setup is off, and we wait for a new hold day before we look to buy again.

reasons: key rests on one proposed card line (x07)
the low-break rule is a proposed criterion (xbk.inv_low_break)

questions.q: What now?
choices: Buy the next day's high anyway
Wait one more day for the trigger
The setup is off
questions.answer: The setup is off
questions.why: The setup is off. A close under the 20 EMA on above-average volume ends it before the trigger.
questions.lesson_line: A heavy close under the 20 EMA ends the idea.

wrong.Buy the next day's high anyway: The setup ended before any trigger.
wrong.Wait one more day for the trigger: The close under the 20 EMA on volume ends it.

questions.story: The hold day looked good. Then the stock closes under its 20 EMA on above-average volume.

questions.q: Kell buys in pieces. Adding a second piece after the crossback buy is part of our plan.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Our plan is one full entry at one price with one stop. Kell buys in pieces. For us, adding or scaling in is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: We buy once at one price. Kell may add; we do not.
questions.simple: No. We buy once at one price with one stop, and we never add.

deeper.trap: The trap is borrowing a famous trader's method whole. Our card lists staggered stops under the 10 and 20 EMA as something we do not do. Our rule is one full entry at one price with one stop. Learn the idea, then trade our rule.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5)

questions.q: What does our plan say?
choices: Add a second piece on the clear
Move the stop under the new low
No add; one price, one stop
questions.answer: No add; one price, one stop
questions.why: No add. A full new entry at one price with one stop: no pilot, no add on follow-through, no staggered stops. Adding or scaling in is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: One price, one stop. Kell may add; we do not.

wrong.Add a second piece on the clear: That is Kell's way, not our plan.
wrong.Move the stop under the new low: The stop only moves up on the plan's own steps.

questions.story: You bought the crossback over the hold day's high at 50.64. Two days later it clears the pop high.

questions.q: Is it a crossback?
choices: No; a Wedge Drop is next
Yes; buy when it touches
Yes, it is the first pullback
No; it is just a Base n' Break
questions.answer: No; a Wedge Drop is next
questions.why: No. After an Exhaustion Extension the next stage in Kell's cycle is a Wedge Drop, not a crossback.
questions.lesson_line: After an Exhaustion Extension, the next stage is a drop, not a crossback.

wrong.Yes, it is the first pullback: After an Exhaustion Extension the next stage is a Wedge Drop, not a crossback.
wrong.Yes; buy when it touches: Buying the touch before buyers show is a named mistake.
wrong.No; it is just a Base n' Break: A Base n' Break is another pullback after a crossback. Here an Exhaustion Extension came first.

questions.story: A stock ran far above its 9 EMA in an Exhaustion Extension. Now it pulls back into its averages.
questions.simple: No. After an Exhaustion Extension the next stage is a drop, not a crossback.

reasons: a proposed card line built on Kell's cycle

questions.q: Buy?
choices: No; it fails the 200-day rule
Yes, at half size with a stop
Yes; the gap-up makes it parabolic
No; wait for a close over the 50-day
questions.answer: No; it fails the 200-day rule
questions.why: No. The rule is no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long. A crossback is not a parabolic long, and the gap-up pop does not make it one. The hold day must close above the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: A textbook shape under the 200-day is still a pass.

wrong.Yes, at half size with a stop: Size does not lift the rule. There are no longs below the 200-day simple moving average.
wrong.Yes; the gap-up makes it parabolic: A crossback is not a parabolic long, so the 200-day rule has no exception here, gap-up or not.

The 50-day
The 200-day
The 20 EMA

Sell it and free the money
Hold; the hold was clean
Move the stop to entry

Sell at 5R, by rule, not before

Keep the old stop at 120.63
The day's close sets the new stop

wrong.Take it at half size for now: Size does not fix a leadership gap.
wrong.Pass; its sales growth is missing: Growth is preferred, but the chart comes first. The story's problem is the RS rating.
wrong.Take it; 72 is nearly a leader: Nearly is not enough. The rule is 80 or more.

questions.story: A clean crossback sets up in a stock with an RS rating of 72.
questions.simple: Pass. Our rule wants an RS rating of 80 or more, and 72 falls short.

deeper.trap: 'Close enough' is how rules wear away. Our line is an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group, and 72 is below it. The exception is parabolic and mean-reversion trades, which are other setups.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C31)

questions.q: What is your call?
choices: Pass; Red means mostly cash
Pass; only Green allows any buys
Buy a small starter position
Short it; Red favors shorts
questions.answer: Pass; Red means mostly cash
questions.why: Pass. In a Red market we hold mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day. A strong stock does not cancel the market reading, and a leader with a crossback is a long.
questions.lesson_line: A great setup in a Red market waits.

wrong.Pass; only Green allows any buys: Yellow allows smaller and fewer buys, and Orange allows A+ only. The reason to pass here is Red.
wrong.Buy a small starter position: Red means mostly cash, and we buy one full entry at one price. There is no pilot.
wrong.Short it; Red favors shorts: Shorts are only for stocks below the 200-day. A leader with a crossback is a long setup.

questions.story: A textbook crossback sets up on a leader. The market reading is Red.
questions.simple: Pass. In a Red market we stay mostly in cash, even when the setup looks perfect.

deeper.counter: The market reading sets how much risk we take, not whether the chart is good. Green is full risk, Yellow smaller and fewer, Orange A+ only, Red mostly cash and shorts. The same setup in a Green market is a different decision.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D46, F65)

questions.q: How does that history affect the grade?
choices: It lowers the grade, a warning
It raises it; a win is due
It matters in a weak market
It bars it from our list
questions.answer: It lowers the grade, a warning
questions.why: It lowers the grade. Repeated failed crossbacks on a stock's own chart are a cue to grade lower. The history is a warning, not a forecast.
questions.lesson_line: A stock with a history of failed crossbacks gets a lower grade.

wrong.It raises it; a win is due: Past failures are a warning, not a reason to expect a win.
wrong.It matters in a weak market: The stock's own failed crossbacks are a cue by themselves, whatever the market does.
wrong.It bars it from our list: It is a cue that lowers the grade, not a ban on the stock.

questions.story: A clean crossback sets up in a stock whose last three crossbacks all failed.
questions.simple: A history of failed crossbacks lowers the grade, because it is a warning sign for the stock.

deeper.trap: The gambler's trap is thinking a win is due. Past failures say this stock's chart has not held its averages, not that a win is owed. Grade it lower and keep the same stop.

reasons: a proposed card cue

questions.q: On our card, which crossback grades higher?
choices: Both crossbacks grade the same
Crossback A, sooner and stronger
Crossback B, because it waited
Crossback B, as it is up 15% already
questions.answer: Crossback A, sooner and stronger
questions.why: Crossback A. Our card counts the first crossback after a powerful pop, a gap on heavy volume, as an A+ cue. Crossback B comes 18 sessions after a 1.0x pop, late in a long advance, which the card grades lower. The card also marks late crossbacks as ones that fail most.
questions.lesson_line: On our card, a strong pop and a short wait grade higher.

wrong.Crossback B, because it waited: A long wait makes the crossback late, and the card grades late crossbacks lower.
wrong.Crossback B, as it is up 15% already: Being up 15% already is not a plus. B also comes 18 sessions after a 1.0x pop, and the card grades late crossbacks lower.
wrong.Both crossbacks grade the same: The card counts the pop and the timing.

questions.story: Crossback A comes 5 sessions after a gap-up pop on 3.6x volume. Crossback B comes 18 sessions after a 1.0x pop, with the stock already up 15% on the quarter.
questions.simple: Crossback A grades higher. It follows a strong pop soon after it, and the card marks late crossbacks lower.

deeper.trap: Lateness and pop strength are grade cues, not gates. A clean-looking crossback can still fail. MU did: it looked clean, simply failed, and the stop did its job. The stop decides.

reasons: the pop window is still open (D-076)
'late fails most' is the card's line; our own scan did not confirm it
the A+ and B grade cues are the card's, not measured on our data
flagged for the owner

questions.q: On our card, a rising 200-day is a grade cue, not a gate.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Our card prefers the 200-day rising, meaning higher than it was 20 sessions ago. That is a grade cue, not a gate. The gate is that the hold day closes above the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: A rising 200-day helps the grade. It is not a gate.
questions.simple: Yes, a rising 200-day line is a grade cue on our card, but it is not a gate.

deeper.trap: A rising 200-day is a grade cue, not a gate. The only gate is that the hold day closes above the 200-day. A stock above a falling 200-day can pass the gate, but it earns less credit on the grade.

reasons: one cited fact only (x33)
the rising 200-day is a proposed criterion (xbk.ma200_rising)

questions.q: A hold day just closed. Read the chart. Take it or pass?
choices: Take it; the hold day is strong
Take it; buy at the day's close
Pass; wait for a close over the high
Pass; the gap makes it too risky
questions.answer: Take it; the hold day is strong
questions.why: Take it. The pop came on an earnings gap. The pullback was a 3-day drift to the 20 EMA, and the hold day closed near its high. That is a clean hold day, judged before the trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Check the close before the trigger: upper half, over the 20 EMA.

wrong.Take it; buy at the day's close: We buy the trade over the hold day's high, never at the close.
wrong.Pass; wait for a close over the high: We buy the trade through the high, at market. We do not wait for a later close.
wrong.Pass; the gap makes it too risky: A gap on heavy volume is a plus for the grade, not a reason to pass.

questions.simple: Take it. The hold day closed strong over the 20 EMA, which is what we need before the trigger.

deeper.trap: The trap is hindsight. This trade ran past 3R on the trigger day. But in our scan 28.9% of crossbacks reached 3R before the stop, and 82.6% hit the stop at some point. Judge the hold day before the trigger, not the result.

reasons: the key is read from a dossier row and a chart, not a rule quote
the chart's bars were not re-checked in this pass

questions.q: A hold day just closed. Read the chart. Take it or pass?
choices: Pass; it closed near the low
Pass; the low missed the zone
Take it; the low reached the zone
Take it; buy at today's close
questions.answer: Pass; it closed near the low
questions.why: Pass. The hold day closed in the lower 3% of its range, not the upper half. The low reached the zone, but the close gave it back. It still reached 3R before the stop, which is luck, not the setup.
questions.lesson_line: A touch of the zone is not enough. The close must be strong.

wrong.Take it; the low reached the zone: The close matters as much as the low. A close in the lower 3% of the range fails.
wrong.Pass; the low missed the zone: The low did reach the zone. The close gave it back.
wrong.Take it; buy at today's close: The hold day is weak. And we buy the trade over the hold day's high, never at the close.

questions.simple: Pass. The hold day closed near the low of its range, and a hold day must close in the upper half.

deeper.trap: The hindsight trap: this near-miss still reached 3R (best 3.5R) before the stop. That was luck. A pass is judged by the setup on the day, not by what came after.

reasons: the key is read from a dossier near-miss row and a chart
the strong-close line is a proposed criterion

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Use the poster's entry, set your stop
Copy the poster's stop and size
Buy a starter now and check later
Build your own entry, stop and size
questions.answer: Build your own entry, stop and size
questions.why: Build your own entry, stop and size. Never take a trade from an alert, a post or a video without your own entry, stop and size by these rules. That starts with checking the hold day yourself. Every planned buy has its entry, stop and size written down before the market opens.
questions.lesson_line: Someone else's alert is not a plan. Build your own entry, stop and size.

wrong.Use the poster's entry, set your stop: The entry must be yours too. Never take a trade from a post without your own entry, stop and size.
wrong.Copy the poster's stop and size: The stop and size must be your own, by our rules.
wrong.Buy a starter now and check later: Entry, stop and size are written down before the market opens, not after the buy.

questions.story: A post says a stock is on its EMA Crossback right now. It gives an entry, a stop and a size.
questions.simple: Do not trade from a post. Build your own entry, stop and size first.

deeper.trap: A post can name the right pattern and still miss the hold day, the stop or the size. Only your own entry, stop and size make it a plan, so the hold day check comes before any order.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F66 and D39)
fixed before (the old choice said check the base)

questions.q: What is your call?
choices: Take it with a tighter stop
Pass; the 9 slipped under the 20
Take it; the hold day is strong
questions.answer: Pass; the 9 slipped under the 20
questions.why: Pass. With the 9 EMA under the 20, there is no reason to be long, even if the hold day closes strong.
questions.lesson_line: A strong hold day does not repair crossed averages.

wrong.Take it; the hold day is strong: A strong close does not fix the averages.
wrong.Take it with a tighter stop: Pulling the stop in to fit the size is a trap.

questions.story: A leader above its 200-day pops, then pulls back. During the pullback the 9 EMA slips under the 20. The hold day closes strong.

questions.q: What does it tell you about the market?
choices: Buy more; they are cheap now
Be careful; risk appetite is weak
Nothing; each stock stands alone
Good sign; weak holders are shaken out
questions.answer: Be careful; risk appetite is weak
questions.why: Be careful. Many crossbacks triggering and failing on low volume across the market is a sign of weak risk appetite. It is a cue to grade crossbacks lower.
questions.lesson_line: When crossbacks keep failing around the market, grade lower.

wrong.Buy more; they are cheap now: Failures around the market are a warning, not a bargain.
wrong.Nothing; each stock stands alone: The market's pattern is part of the context.
wrong.Good sign; weak holders are shaken out: Many failures on low volume point to weak risk appetite, not a clean-out. It is a cue to grade lower.

questions.story: Over two weeks, many crossbacks across the market trigger and fail on low volume.
questions.simple: Be careful. Crossbacks failing across the market on low volume point to weak risk appetite.

deeper.counter: One clean crossback can still work. The cue lowers the grade and does not forbid the trade. Check both the stock's own history and how this setup has done across the market lately.

reasons: a proposed card cue built on a market-wide read

questions.q: What do you do about the stop?
choices: Keep the honest stop; cut size or skip
Pull the stop in to fit
Widen the stop
questions.answer: Keep the honest stop; cut size or skip
questions.why: Keep the honest stop. If it does not fit the risk, cut the size or skip. The stop only moves up, never wider.
questions.lesson_line: The stop does not bend to fit the size. The size bends to the stop.

wrong.Widen the stop: The stop only moves up, never wider.
wrong.Pull the stop in to fit: Pulling the stop in to fit the size is a trap.

questions.story: The honest stop is wider than your risk budget allows. A friend says to give it more room.

questions.q: Which pullback is the better crossback?
choices: Neither; both are the same
The gentle, sideways drift
The hard drop; it is quicker
The drop; it clears sellers
questions.answer: The gentle, sideways drift
questions.why: The gentle drift. Kell says the crossback works best when price gently moves sideways and the averages rise to meet it. TraderLion, describing his method, adds that a slow drift into the averages is ideal and that the cleaner, shallower pullback is better.
questions.lesson_line: Let the averages rise to price. A gentle drift beats a violent drop.

wrong.Neither; both are the same: The cleaner and shallower pullback is better.
wrong.The hard drop; it is quicker: Speed is not the point. The averages need time to rise.
wrong.The drop; it clears sellers: TraderLion says a slow drift is ideal and the cleaner, shallower pullback is better. A hard drop is not that.

questions.story: Two stocks pop and then pull back to their averages. One holds a narrow range for five sessions. The other drops hard in two.
questions.simple: The slow drift is better. It lets the averages rise up to meet price.

deeper.example: In our examples, CLS drifted four quiet sessions and ALGN drifted six sessions with its low exactly on the 20 EMA. Both were slow, quiet pullbacks. A hard two-day drop gives the averages no time to rise.

reasons: Kell and TraderLion agree

questions.q: We buy a crossback with a market order the moment the trigger trades, in regular hours.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Entries are market orders, placed the moment price trades over the trigger, and only in regular hours.
questions.lesson_line: Market order at the trigger, regular hours only.
questions.simple: Yes. We buy with a market order as soon as price trades over the trigger, and only in regular hours.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, E58)

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: It is 8:10 am, before the open. A thin pre-market print takes the stock a few cents over the hold day's high.
choices: Wait; only regular hours can trigger
Buy at market now, before it runs away
Rest a limit order at the high now
Skip it; a pre-market print kills it
questions.answer: Wait; only regular hours can trigger
questions.why: Wait. No new buys outside regular hours, and entries are market orders. If the trigger trades after the open, buy then.
questions.lesson_line: A pre-market print is not your trigger. Regular hours only.

wrong.Buy at market now, before it runs away: Pre-market is outside regular hours. The rule is no new buys there.
wrong.Rest a limit order at the high now: Entries are market orders, bought in regular hours. A resting order is not our entry.
wrong.Skip it; a pre-market print kills it: A thin pre-market print does not turn the setup off. It stays on until the hold day's low breaks or the window runs out.

questions.simple: Wait for regular hours. A pre-market print is not a trigger, and we only buy at market in regular hours.

deeper.trap: The print is thin, and thin pre-market trades are not our entry. Our trigger is price trading over the hold day's high in regular hours, with a market order the moment it does.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, E58)

questions.q: A crossback trigger gaps and would fill at 54.60. The 9 EMA is 49.00. How far above it, in percent?
questions.why: 11.4%. The fill is above the average by (54.60 - 49.00) / 49.00 = 11.4%. That is more than 10% above the 9 EMA, so we skip it as too stretched to buy.
questions.lesson_line: More than 10% over the 9 EMA is a chase. Skip it.
questions.simple: The fill is 11.4% above the 9 EMA, which is past the 10% limit, so we skip it.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (C29, the 10% stretch rule)

wrong.5.6%: Used the dollar gap as if it were the percent.
wrong.10.3%: Divided the gap by the fill, not by the 9 EMA.
wrong.1.1%: A decimal slip, one place too far left.

questions.q: Which rule says to skip this buy?
questions.story: The hold day's high was 100.00, and the 9 EMA is 93.00. The stock sits well above its 200-day. It opens next morning at 103.00, so a market buy fills near there.
choices: The 10% stretch rule
The 4% chase limit
The 200-day rule
The 3-session rule
questions.answer: The 10% stretch rule
questions.why: The 10% stretch rule. A long more than 10% above its 9 EMA is too stretched to buy. Here 103.00 is more than 10% above the 93.00 average. The fill is only a little over the 100.00 high, so the 4% chase limit passes. The stock is well above its 200-day, and the buy comes the next morning, inside the 3 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Two checks at the fill: distance from the trigger and distance from the 9 EMA.

wrong.The 4% chase limit: The fill is a little over the trigger, so the chase limit passes. The stretch rule is the one that fails.
wrong.The 200-day rule: The stock sits well above its 200-day, so that rule passes.
wrong.The 3-session rule: The buy comes the next morning, one session after the hold day. That is inside the 3 sessions.

questions.simple: The fill is more than 10% above the 9 EMA, so the stretch rule says skip.

deeper.example: Walk through it. The fill, 103.00, is a little over the 100.00 high, so the 4% limit passes. The 9 EMA is 93.00, and 103.00 is more than 10% above it, so the 10% rule fails. Both checks run at the fill, and either one can say skip.

reasons: computed comparison (101.50 against the 91.00 average)
rests on the owner's rulebook (C29 and C28)
fixed before (the old story had the wrong prices)

questions.q: A crossback stock trades 4,000,000 shares a day on average. What is the most shares our volume rule lets us hold?
questions.answer: 40,000 shares
questions.why: 40,000 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 4,000,000 x 0.01 = 40,000. The risk math or the position cap may allow more, but this ceiling still holds.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of the average daily volume is the ceiling.
questions.simple: Our rule caps us at 1% of the average daily volume, which is 40,000 shares here.

reasons: one cited fact only (h19)
computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)

choices: 40,000 shares
400,000 shares
80,000 shares
4,000,000 shares

wrong.400,000 shares: Took ten times the right share of the volume.
wrong.80,000 shares: Doubled the 1% rule. The ceiling is 1% of the average daily volume.
wrong.4,000,000 shares: Used the whole average daily volume as the limit.

questions.q: A textbook crossback does not lift our limit on how much of the daily volume we may own.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and illiquid stocks are not even watched. A clean chart does not lift the ceiling.
questions.lesson_line: A clean chart does not lift the volume ceiling.
questions.simple: Yes, a clean chart does not change the rule that we never own more than 1% of daily volume.

reasons: one cited fact only (h19)
rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Every position has a real stop order with the ___, not a stop kept in your head.
questions.answer: broker
questions.why: Broker. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head. Only an order placed with the broker is a real stop.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head is not a stop. Place a real one with the broker.
questions.simple: A stop must be a real order with your broker, not something you only keep in your head.

reasons: one cited fact only (h18)
rests on the owner's rulebook (D41)

questions.q: Once the crossback stop is set, it only moves up. The one exception is the gap rule.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The stop is the exit and it only moves up, never down or wider. The gap rule is the one exception. Every position also has a real stop order with the broker.
questions.lesson_line: Set the stop before the buy. It only goes up from there.
questions.simple: Yes. Once set, the stop only moves up, and the gap rule is the one exception.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, B20)

questions.q: We pass on a clean crossback when the latest sales and earnings are not growing.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Growing sales and earnings are preferred, but the chart comes first. Weak growth alone does not make us pass a clean crossback.
questions.lesson_line: Growth helps the grade. The chart still decides.
questions.simple: No. We prefer growing sales and earnings, but the chart comes first.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D40)

questions.q: Bought at 40.82, stop 40.17. What is the earliest price the stop may go to breakeven?
questions.why: $42.12. One R is the fill minus the stop: 40.82 - 40.17. Breakeven comes at 2R: 40.82 + 2 x (40.82 - 40.17) = 42.12. The rule allows breakeven anywhere from 2R to 5R, so 2R is the earliest.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R. From 2R the stop can move up to your entry.
questions.simple: The stop may go to breakeven once the trade reaches 2R, which is 42.12 here.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, breakeven from 2R)

wrong.$41.47: That is one R up, too early. The earliest breakeven is 2R.
wrong.$40.82: That is the fill, where the stop goes. It is not the trigger price.
wrong.$39.52: That subtracts two R from the fill instead of adding it.

questions.story: Bought on the trigger day.

questions.q: From which R can the crossback stop go to breakeven?
choices: From 2R, any time up to 5R
From 1R, once it moves up
Only at 5R, never sooner
From the first higher close
questions.answer: From 2R, any time up to 5R
questions.why: From 2R. The rule allows moving the stop to breakeven anywhere from 2R to 5R. It does not start sooner.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, not before.

wrong.From 1R, once it moves up: Too soon. The rule starts at 2R.
wrong.Only at 5R, never sooner: 5R is the far end of the range, not the only point. The rule allows 2R to 5R.
wrong.From the first higher close: A close is not a measure of R. The move is set in R, from 2R.

questions.simple: Breakeven is allowed from 2R up to 5R, and not before 2R.

reasons: the breakeven range comes from the card

questions.story: Bought on the trigger day at 136.18 with the stop at 134.80.

questions.q: You hold 120 shares, sell 30 at a first sell and 50 more at a later sell. How many shares are left to trail?

questions.lesson_line: Add up what you sold. What is left is what you trail.
questions.simple: The two sells take 80 shares, so 120 minus 80 leaves 40 shares to trail.

when each sell comes is the owner's D-013 judgment

choices: 90 shares
80 shares
70 shares
40 shares

wrong.80 shares: That is the amount sold, not what is left.
wrong.90 shares: Took off the first sell only.
wrong.70 shares: Took off the later sell only.

questions.why: Day 3. We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy and usually wait until day 3 at the earliest. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R.
questions.lesson_line: Rarely sell on day 1. Day 3 at the earliest.
questions.simple: We rarely sell on day 1 and usually wait until day 3 at the earliest.

reasons: rests on the owner's ruling D-013 (day 3 at the earliest)

wrong.1: We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy.
wrong.5: Day 5 is inside the push we sell into, but we do not wait that long at the earliest.

questions.q: Our rule for a climax run on your long: what is the move?
questions.story: Your crossback winner has run four days straight, gapping up each morning, now far above its 9 EMA.
choices: Sell a big part into the run
Sell a small part and trail the rest
Add a third piece into strength
Hold all of it and trail the 9 EMA
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the run
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. Our rule for a climax run far above the 9 EMA on your own long is to sell a big part. It is a judgment call. We never add, because we buy once at one price with one stop.
questions.lesson_line: A climax run is a place to sell a big part, not to add.

wrong.Add a third piece into strength: We buy once at one price with one stop and never add. A climax run is a place to sell.
wrong.Sell a small part and trail the rest: The rule says sell a big part into a climax run, not a small one.
wrong.Hold all of it and trail the 9 EMA: The trail is the default for the rest. Into a climax run the rule is to sell a big part first.

questions.simple: Sell a big part into the run, because a climax run far above the 9 EMA is a place to sell.

deeper.trap: The trap is the winner's pride. A run like this feels like proof to hold everything or to add. Our rule is the opposite: sell a big part into a climax run. Adding is never the answer, because we buy once, at one price with one stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C34), a judgment call
the exact share to sell is left to judgment

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The hold day's low may trade down to about ___ under the 20 EMA.
questions.why: 1%. The zone runs from the 9 EMA down to about 1% under the 20 EMA. A low deeper than that is outside the zone, and the day is not a hold day.
questions.lesson_line: The zone stops about 1% under the 20 EMA.

wrong.3%: That is closer to how wide a stop usually sits, not how deep the low may go. The zone ends about 1% under the 20 EMA.
wrong.5%: That is far deeper than the zone, which ends about 1% under the 20 EMA.
wrong.10%: That belongs to a different rule, how far a buy may stretch above its short average. The zone ends about 1% under the 20 EMA.

questions.simple: The hold day's low can dip about 1% under the 20 EMA and still count.

questions.story: A hold day just closed. The stock drifted into its 9/20 zone and printed a strong hold day. The Nasdaq 100 closed under its own 20-day EMA today.
questions.q: On our card, what does the index cue say about this trade?
choices: It lowers the grade but does not block
It blocks the buy until index heals
Nothing, only the chart counts
Raises the grade, the stock leads

questions.why: It lowers the grade but does not block. On our card the index is a cue, not a gate. The cue is met when the Nasdaq is not below its 20-day EMA, or a market Wedge Pop has just happened. The Nasdaq is below it here, so the cue is not met and the grade drops. Kell himself trades less or smaller when the index is below its 20 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: The index is a cue, not a gate. Under its 20-day EMA, the grade drops.

wrong.It blocks the buy until index heals: On our card the index is a cue, not a gate. It lowers the grade but does not block the buy.
wrong.Nothing, only the chart counts: The card lists the market under its 20-day EMA as a lower-grade cue. Kell also trades less in index corrections.
wrong.Raises the grade, the stock leads: The card lists the market under its 20-day EMA as a lower-grade cue. A market Wedge Pop is the cue that helps.

questions.simple: On our card a Nasdaq under its 20-day EMA lowers the grade but does not block the trade.

the card's evidence cites D-023's default that no setup adds its own index filter, and the owner has not ruled

questions.q: You buy a crossback. Where does your stop live?
choices: A real stop order with your broker
In your head, with the screen watched
As a phone alert at the hold day's low
In your journal as a planned exit
questions.answer: A real stop order with your broker
questions.why: A real stop order with your broker. Only an order placed with the broker is a real stop. A stop kept in your head or an alert only works if you are watching and act at once. Place the real stop right after the buy.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head is not a stop. Place a real one with the broker.

wrong.In your head, with the screen watched: A stop kept in your head is not a stop. It only works if you are watching and act.
